ak_good_vibes_wall.blurb: A roadside amphitheater beside the Seward Highway on Turnagain Arm, just south of Anchorage and close to sea level. Fifteen routes, about two-thirds bolted and the rest trad, run from 5.7 up to the 5.12 range, with a fairly even spread from 5.9 through 5.12. A few lines are short two-pitch outings, which is unusual for this stretch of highway. The stone is rough and loose by Turnagain Arm standards, so wear a helmet and place gear often. Surf and passing traffic make it hard to talk to your partner, and it is quieter late in the evening during the long summer days. A handy after-work stop.

ak_bermuda_triangle.blurb: A compact crag right beside the Seward Highway on Turnagain Arm, a few miles south of Anchorage and just short of Beluga Point. It is named for a triangular overhanging corner. Fifteen routes are packed into a small space: mostly bolted lines plus a handful of trad cracks, from an easy 5.5 up to the 5.11 range, with the biggest cluster at 5.11 and another at 5.10. Expect loose rock, bolting and anchors of mixed quality, and plenty of road noise, so a helmet is wise. A convenient short session for a climber who wants an easy trad crack or a few moderate to hard sport pitches.

ak_resolution_bluff.blurb: A mixed crag set back from the Seward Highway near McHugh Creek on Turnagain Arm, reached on foot rather than from a roadside pullout. Its fifteen routes include trad lines, bolted sport routes and a couple of top-rope cracks, spanning 5.8 to 5.12 with most sitting between 5.10 and 5.11. Bring a single rack of cams for the crack lines. It catches sun through much of the day, feels secluded, and is far quieter than the roadside walls, which makes it a pleasant pick when you want a calmer outing close to Anchorage. Hardware is stainless steel.

ak_morning_star_gully.blurb: A steep gully on the Seward Highway just beyond Beluga Point, south of Anchorage. It faces east, so it warms up early in the day, and the walls shelter you from wind. The rock is better than average for the highway. Of fifteen routes, most are bolted, a few are trad and there is one boulder problem; grades start around 5.8 and are concentrated at 5.10 and 5.11. The way in cuts through dense brush, with prickly cow parsnip and devil's club that are worst in wet summers and ease off in spring and fall. A good morning choice for sport climbers working the 5.10s.

ak_panorama_point.blurb: A small cliff above the east end of the Valdez airstrip, the highest of a group of four walls there. The reward is a wide outlook over the valley, the harbor and the glacier-topped peaks. It has fifteen routes, mostly bolted or mixed-protection lines on blank faces with small crimps, open-book corners and ledge traverses, graded from 5.6 up into the 5.12 range. The walk up from the end of the campground road is short and steep, roughly a quarter of an hour, and passes the base of the neighboring Lookout Rock on the way.

ak_snowbird_slab_cornerstone.blurb: A moderate-friendly crag in the Reed Lakes basin of Hatcher Pass, north of Palmer, perched at about 3,200 feet. Fifteen routes mix trad (the larger share), bolted sport lines and one top-rope, with grades from 5.6 up to 5.10, and a few of the longer routes go multi-pitch, including two of four pitches. It is a solid choice for a full day or an evening of enjoyable moderate climbing. Hardware has been upgraded to stainless, and most lines have rings for lowering. Getting there takes a walk of roughly two miles up the valley past an old cabin, so pack for changing mountain weather.

ak_3rd_fin.blurb: One of a row of coastal fins at Jaw Point, about fifteen miles south of Juneau on the water, so a boat is the way to reach it. The fin is mostly a trad crag, with nine trad lines, three bolted routes and two boulder problems among fourteen climbs. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.14, with a strong cluster in the 5.11 range, while an easy 5.8 corner and a moderate chimney line offer a gentler way up. Several routes here are among the best-rated on the Fins. This is remote, uncrowded cragging in a Southeast Alaska setting.
